speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 20 years ago the federal government established the National Arts Centre as Canada's national cultural institution. As Maureen Forrester, immediate past chair of the board, stated, "The formation of the NAC is arguably the most important single artistic development ever to occur in Canada's national capital".
Since its inception, several notables have been in such positions as director general, artistic director and on the board of trustees. Up until two years ago the centre's principals worked together to create one of Canada's finest institutions. Recently, patrons of the NAC have been asking people to sign petitions which accuse the new management of the NAC of being cavalier, incompetent and inadequate in artistic matters. It is for these reasons that I call on the Minister of Communications to initiate a public inquiry into the affairs of running the National Arts Centre. The inquiry must look into what has happened of late to bring the centre, its staff, its programming, and its orchestra to such an all-time low.
It is imperative that we address these problems before a major institution is destroyed and a wonderful orchestra becomes a thing of the past.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the director of Carrefour Inc.,
located in UAvenir, in my riding, and I am referring to Mr. Rene McKaye and his team who received an award last Friday in the "development" category, one of the Coeur-du-Quebec 1989 tourism awards, for improving and developing their infrastructures.
I am also delighted that the Canadian Government was involved in this success thanks to its contribution through the special Laprade region program, which contributed $350,000.
Established in 1954 with the help of volunteers, this vacation centre, located in a magnificent setting on a hillside overlooking the Saint-Franco is river, has changed considerably since those early years.
With its new infrastructures, Carrefour Inc. should now be considered a full-fledged resort.
Since Carrefour is open the year round, tourists, businesses and organizations that want to meet in a setting conducive to work and relaxation are able to take advantage of the many services and activities it offers.
This enterprise is to be commended for its determination, dynamic approach and sense of entrepreneurship in developing regional and provincial tourism.

Mr. Speaker, I want to point out how well the Conservative Government understands the farmers of Canada and Quebec.
My Government listens to farmers. Last week, the president of the UPA (Quebec farmers' union), Mr. Proulx, and his officials met with our Ministers of Agriculture, the Minister for International Trade and the Prime Minister.
The federal Government has just granted Quebec pork producers $48 million under the stabilization program and, together with their federation, we are continuing the fight to abolish the countervailing duties imposed by the United States.

For milk producers, we abolished the milk price freeze and granted an increase of 47 cents per hectolitre.
We will make GATT see the light about yogourt and ice cream, Mr. Speaker. We want to strengthen Article XI of GATT, which fully protects us from certain imports.
The Hon. Member for Beauce is a strong defender of Quebec agriculture. We believe in the value of our marketing boards, our joint plans and our quotas!
Our farmers have made sacrifices, got organized and disciplined themselves. Believe me, we will protect ourselves!
The Conservative Members from Quebec are attentive and alert and my Government understands agriculture.

Mr. Speaker, today I have the great pleasure of welcoming a new premier into the Canadian constitutional family. Not only a new premier but a Social Democrat premier.
Yesterday, celebrating the tenth anniversary of responsible government in the Yukon, and acting upon the authority granted to the Yukon by a Progressive Conservative Government, the hon. Tony Penikett abolished the title "Government Leader" and instituted the title of "Premier".
Authority for this action was expressly granted on October 10,1979, by the Minister of Northern and Indian Affairs.
As Premier Penikett stated: "The colonial title of government leader is not recognized anywhere outside of the north."
I welcome this New Democrat premier into the fold. I trust that the Prime Minister will do the same and that we will, finally, see the duly elected leader of the Yukon
government as an active participant in all First Ministers conferences.
Hear, hear!

ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE DRESS CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with considerable sadness that I rise today to ask Canadians for tolerance and understanding on an issue of great concern to many.
As you know, numerous petitions have recently been filed with this House regarding the allowance of cultural dress and religious symbols in the code of dress of the RCMP. These petitions and the related controversy have given rise to unfortunate incidents of prejudice and racism that are directed at the Sikh community.
We all must and I am sure do deplore and condemn this intolerance and prejudice. This is fundamentally an argument about human rights, cultural identity and the very nature of our multicultural mosaic. Racism has no place.
The Sikh community has a long tradition of living in harmony with other cultures all over the world. I am sure that men of good will can resolve this issue in a way which is consistent with our Charter of Rights and in a way that also celebrates not only our cultural diversity but also the traditions that unite all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, today, the United Nations Day of Solidarity with South African political prisoners, I wish to take this opportunity to remember the thousands of political prisoners who have been imprisoned in South Africa for their struggle against the racist policies of apartheid. Last night, South African president de Klerk announced the immediate release of eight long-term political prisoners, the desired effect obviously being to deflect criticism during the upcoming Commonwealth Conference. This action is to be applauded but it is insufficient.
The release of eight prisoners who have served up to 26 years in jail in South Africa does not represent the end to the policy of apartheid in South Africa. South
October 11, 1989

Africa has just come through a national election where not one black person was able to vote, this in a population whose majority is black.
Four years ago, before the United Nations General Assembly, the Prime Minister committed to increased sanctions against South Africa if apartheid was not dismantled. Apartheid is still alive and well in South Africa and those opposed to apartheid in South Africa urge Canada and other nations to step up the pressure not decrease it. Sanctions are working. Do not stop now.
Today, in particular, we must remember the hundreds of political prisoners who yet remain imprisoned in South Africa and their struggle to overthrow the oppression of the apartheid system. Canada must represent their interests before the Heads of State Commonwealth Conference and exemplify its own commitment to continue to fight apartheid by furthering sanctions now.

Mr. Speaker, today I would like to point out to the House the excellent performance of Tembec Inc., a pulp and paper company located in Temiscamingue, in my riding. Tembec was chosen for one of the 1989 Canadian export awards of excellence. For Tembec, Mr. Speaker, that is a well-deserved honour which is due to the dynamism of its president, Frank Dottori, and a staff of remarkable ability.
This Canadian export award of excellence honours Canadian companies that not only increased their exports but also exported new products successfully or reached new markets.
The winners are chosen from among hundreds of candidates by a selection board made up of Canadian personalities, in particular, business people, union leaders, journalists and officials of the Department of External Affairs and of International Trade Canada.
So, Mr. Speaker, I congratulate Tembec, its president and all'its employees!

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has anointed himself the "Education Prime Minister". In a speech to the Conservative party in August, the Prime Minister proclaimed that: "this government will carry its fair share of the burden to ensure that all young Canadians receive a first class education as they confront a world class challenge".
The Prime Minister also said that education will be a high priority at the next First Ministers' Conference, and he would advocate a collective study of Canada's education system.
These are admirable goals, but unfortunately the reality of this government's commitment to higher education is totally inadequate. This week the government will introduce Bill C-33, which will slash federal expenditure on education by $650 million over the next five years. When the effects of the last cuts by this government in 1986 are included the totals are staggering. Over a nine year period, between 1986 to 1994, this government led by an education Prime Minister will cut close to $7 billion from federal transfers devoted to post-secondary education.
Yesterday, to add insult to injury, a senior federal official was quoted as saying that education discussions with the provinces are to be held in private because: "What we are going to say about it, you are not going to want to hear in public".
On behalf of all Canadians who support the improvement of higher education in Canada, I demand that the First Ministers discussion take place in public and that this government immediately withdraw the destructive Bill C-33.

Mr. Speaker, Manitoba's historic role as a Canadian transportation centre is eroding. Over 3,000 CN and CP employees have lost their jobs in Manitoba over the last eight years. The recent savage cuts in VIA Rail will hasten this erosion. This is appalling since Manitoba has major

October 11, 1989
Oral Questions
advantages as a transportation hub. It is located at the geographic centre of the country and has strong representation of both federally owned and private transportation companies.
The federal and Manitoba governments acknowledged the importance of Manitoba's transportation sector in 1984 when they initiated two transportation agreements. But these agreements are expiring with no renewal of commitment. Maintaining Manitoba as a transportation centre is vital not only to the well-being of Manitobans, but also to the provision of efficient transportation to all Canadians. Nothing will fill the void. Thus I urge the government to take action to repair the damage and restore Manitoba's rightful role as a Canadian transportation centre.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Wine Institute, composed of 17 companies, operating 30 wineries and representing 80 per cent of Canadian wine producers, has recently announced its support in principle of the proposed goods and services tax.
The wine industry has been adversely affected under the current federal sales tax which is applied at the manufacturer's level. Subsequent tax cascading results in an inflated price for Canadian wine. Given the current rates of excise tax and provincial mark-up levels, Canadian wines would be more affordable once the GST was in place. As a result, domestic wines would be much more competitive with imports.
In the past, individuals have expressed concerns about the wine industry's ability to compete in the world market. We should continue this concern and give the wine industry the ability to compete in the international marketplace. Replacing the federal sales tax will enhance its capacity to do so by making Canadian wines more affordable for consumers

Mr. Speaker, when I listen to the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Juan
de Fuca, Mr. David Barrett, who is running for the leadership of the New Democratic Party, I am astounded at the Hon. Member's failure to understand what Quebec is all about and at his lack of political maturity in wanting to capitalize on anti-French sentiment.
I think he would do well to visit the people of Quebec and listen to what they have to say.
If he does, he will be surprised at the vast movement that is forming today in Quebec. Independence is no longer the sole concern of people in the Parti Quebecois.
For several weeks, provincial and federal Liberals have been coming to see us, and they say that if the Anglophones turn us down, this time it will be independence.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca is running for the leadership of one of Canada's political parties, but if he doesn't change his approach, he may well become the leader of a political party without a country.

I am sure all Members appreciate Mr. Douglas' good will. However, does our Minister of Finance realize that after the goods and services tax was introduced in New Zealand in October 1986, New Zealand registered a negative growth rate; New Zealand went into a period of economic recession; inflation was over 15 per cent; the cost of food rose 10 per cent in one month; the number of jobs dropped by more than 3 per cent, and finally, New Zealand's exports, which until then had increased by over 9 per cent, dropped by 0.1 per cent?

That's true!
October 11, 1989

Speaking of a tax grab, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport, who has been left out of this current debate.

Mr. Speaker-

I see the Minister of Communications here and I would like to put a question to him. I am surprised he is not in Hollywood as an advance man for the Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, we ought to note in this House that artists, orchestras, dance troupes, opera companies, playwrights and regional theatres will all be hammered by this 9 per cent tax. According to a study prepared for the Canada Council by Woods, Gordon Consultants reporting to the minister, performing arts organizations will pay up to seven times more federal tax than they currently pay.
Why has the Minister of Communications not done anything to keep Canadian cultural groups from being wiped out by this tax Why is the Minister allowing his colleague to impose a tax on the future Karen Kains, k.d. langs, the Denys Arcands, the Robert Batemans, the Gilles Vigneaults and Anne Murrays of this country? Why has he not stood up for the artistic community in this country to protect our Canadian identity?

Mr. Speaker, my Department has been examining and analysing this matter for several months. I had a chance to discuss the issue with my provincial colleagues in Winnipeg last week, and I gave them the assurance that the Government, in this area as in all others, would act responsibly. In fact we have proved that in other areas since 1984. The cultural sector has increased its percentage of the Government's discretionary spending from 5.4 to 7 percent, and the Government intends to keep up the good work, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister for International Trade. In a speech on October 2, the minister said: "The availability of concessional funding for trade has been instrumental in providing equal footing for our exporters".
Yet today we learn that the government is cancelling the funding for trade. There will be no concessional funding until next April. Can the minister tell us why, at a time when our exports are at a ten-year low when the rate of our dollar is crippling our exports, the government has added another crippling blow in our ability to compete abroad? Will he undertake to explain to his colleague, the Minister of Finance, that exports abroad will create jobs for Canada, will create more wealth and that is the best way to deal with the deficit?
Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International
TVade): Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman forgot to mention in his prologue-I suppose that is what you would call it-that the current account reference levels this year have increased 66 per cent over last year, going up in the Estimates from $75 million to $125 million and I think it is likely there will be supplementary estimates which will further increase that. There is a considerable increase in the spending for export credit financing. We have been doing so well that Canadian exports and the need for support is increased even at a faster rate than the amount of money that the House has voted in the Estimates. So the hon. gentleman's complaint is that we are doing too well.

Mr. Speaker, my complaint is that we are running a current account deficit with every single country in the world. Our exports are at a 10-year low, and our trade market is falling out of the bottom. This government is doing nothing about it.
We want to know why it is, at a time when our so-called favoured trade market has just increased a $100 million war chest to go after our markets with the Pacific Rim while it has had $200 million for additional export financing for agriculture, this government is cancelling concessional financing for our own compan-
October 11, 1989

ies. Are we just surrending finally and getting out with a whimper, or is this government going to stand up for Canadian business for a change?
Mr. Speaker, I suppose we will have to decide whether we want to believe the hon. trade critic for the Official Opposition or whether we want to believe impartial experts, for example-
Like you?

I am an impartial expert, but I will refer to others in my modesty, Mr. Speaker.
There was an article in The Financial Post of September 23, 1989: "Signs point to trade upswing; new export chances will boost Canada's surplus". The picture the hon. gentleman painted is an entirely false picture.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister and the Minister of the Environment, I have a question for the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
Earlier today, simultaneously in Chicago and Toronto, there was an alarming report produced by the Institute for Research on Public Policy jointly with the oldest conservation in the United States. According to this report the situation in the Great Lakes has been getting worse. In their words, there is an environmental crisis and the health of humans as well as that of wildlife continues to be threatened.
Yesterday, in anticipation of this announcement, the minister of health recycled an old election promise by saying that the Conservative government would spend $1 per Canadian per year for the next five years to deal with this crisis. Since the Prime Minister in the election campaign said: "No area is higher on our environmental priority list than the Great Lakes themselves", I want to ask the minister why in that time has the government done nothing in the Great Lakes and what makes him believe that $1 per Canadian per year for the next five years is at all adequate?

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all the premise of the hon. member's question is wrong. We have had programs in
Oral Questions
place for a good deal of time dealing with the Great Lakes.
What this commitment yesterday represents is a doubling of the federal commitment to clean up the Great Lakes. It represents an effort being made to cut down on new pollution going to the Great Lakes. It represents an effort to clean up the 17 hot spots around the Great Lakes in Canadian or binational territory. It represents for the first time a major new effort to get fundamental information that we need about the health effects of pollution in the Great Lakes. The hon. gentleman feels that is not important; I think Canadians will disagree with him, and I think that Canadians will feel that this initiative announced yesterday is of fundamental importance to every Canadian.

Mr. Speaker, the minister's rhetoric is no different from the Prime Minister's. We saw the action that was taken since then and the action is zero. When the government was elected in 1984 there were 17 toxic spots on the Great Lakes. There are 17 today. It hasn't changed one bit. No money was spent on the Great Lakes in the past year to deal with this situation.
My question to the minister is this: Since there are 6 million Canadians drinking the water in the Great Lakes system that according to these reports today leads to birth defects, tumours, and nerve and brain damage on human beings, when is the government going to start delivering the goods? What makes him think that moving from 50 cents per Canadian per year to $1 per Canadian per year is anywhere adequate to deal with the serious problem?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether the hon. gentleman has actually bothered to read the report. I have. I do not know if the hon. gentleman has actually bothered to look at what sort of research has been done to date on health effects, but I can say that my department believes that a new initiative of some $20 million to look at the health effects-
It's peanuts.

"Peanuts", says the hon. gentleman; just $20 million, he says. Don't bother doing it, he says; it is not important. Well, he is wrong.
It is time that Canadians had this sort of information so that we knew exactly what were the threats to specific populations, so that we knew what measures could be taken to protect them, and so that we could ensure that efforts were being made to clean up these environmental

October 11, 1989
Oral Questions
hot spots and that Canadians had conditions in the Great Lakes which enhance human health and which do not threaten human health. We believe this is an important initiative.

Mr. Speaker, I repeat, in the four years leading up to the last election there was nothing done about the 17 spots. This great promise was made in last year's election. There is no greater priority than the Great Lakes and nothing has been done in the year since. The people have given up on the Government of Canada when it comes to the environment.

Mr. Speaker, in the United States, the Environmental Protection Agency published a list of major polluters, and as a result, because of this humiliating disclosure, some of these polluters, have changed their practices. Will the Canadian Government publish a similar list here in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me first correct the hon. gentleman, if he has any interest in facts. He says that nothing has been done with regard to those environmental hot spots around the Great Lakes. That is simply false.
The hon. gentleman should know full well, if he does not, that the amendment to the 1978 Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement, the 1987 Protocol which was negotiated by Canada and pressed for by Canada, was designed to put the responsibility on both governments on both sides of the lakes to clean up these hot spots and to take further action. That is exactly what we have been doing. We have been putting in place remedial action plans.
One of these hot spots-
The situation is getting worse, not better.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman screams across his suggestions about what we should be doing. Let me suggest to him that he listen for a minute because he obviously is in need of facts.
In this fund we have set aside there is money for cleaning up those hot spots. There is money to be put in
place to prevent pollution of the Great Lakes. There is money to be put in place to ensure that we have information about the environmental threat to human health. Members of the NDP says that doubling the federal effort is inconsequential. I think they are wrong, and I think this initiative is important for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of National Health and Welfare and it also deals with the recycled garbage that the government is parading as environmental policy.
I would like to refer the hon. minister to a statement made by the Prime Minister in Hamilton one year ago when he was on the election trail. He stated that of the $125 million being set aside for the Great Lakes action plan $75 million would be spent specifically on cleaning up the 17 hot spots. In the minister's own statement yesterday on page 3 that amount has shrunk to $55 million, a $20 million drop in the amount of money being spent to clean up the Great Lakes.
I would like to ask the minister who authorized the $20 million cut and, if there is a need for a study, why did he not add $20 million as a separate add-on in light of the potential for brain damage and the other incredibly disturbing evidence we have seen in the report tabled today?
Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and
Welfare): Mr. Speaker, the hon. member refers to this announcement of $125 million being committed to Great Lakes clean up as recycled garbage. It is $125 million more than the Liberal government was prepared to put into cleaning up the Great Lakes. All that we had was talk from them.
Hear, hear!

That's right, it's not cleaning up.

Again the hon. member shouts from her seat. Perhaps she could listen. We created a $20 million health effects program which was designed to give us the very sort of information the hon. member alleges she has already and does not need. We also indicated that we are

prepared to add to that fund after 1992 if it is necessary to do so in the clean up of those 17 hot spots.

He may laugh about the fact that 9 million Canadians are drinking water that could lead their children to brain damage. Of course I have a concern. I have had a concern and consideration for many more years, and I do not need the minister's lectures.

He is doing a tour of the Rhine wine valley and he is studying pollution in Paris. Where is the Minister of the Environment of Canada when he is confronted with one of the most disturbing studies in the history of the Great Lakes? He is off studying the Rhine pollution problems and pollution in Paris. I would like to know where the minister is.

If the hon. member knew anything about the environment she would know that the environment is an international matter that requires concerted international action. We believe that the efforts of the Minister of the Environment in Europe are essential in terms of encouraging concerted international efforts to protect Canada's environment.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport who announced the VIA cuts last week and who announced the cut in the Canadian.
Across northern Ontario there are two rail lines. The rail line chosen to continue this passage across northern Ontario was a CN line that services a population of about 5,000 people. This decision eliminates passenger rail service on the CP line from Sudbury to Chapleau, White River, Marathon, Nipigon, Thunder Bay, Dryden, Kenora, and on to Winnipeg. The route services a population of over 350,000 people.
This decision is obviously an error: servicing 5,000 people instead of 350,000 people across northern Ontario. If the minister persists in going ahead with the VIA cuts, will he at least agree to use the route that services the most people across northern Ontario?

In the case of northern Ontario we have to consider that there are a few communities that do not have any other mode of transportation while in Thunder Bay and in Sudbury, we have good air transportation, roads, and so on. He understands very well that in the decision that we made we considered that it was better at the time to keep the service for what we called the remote commu-

nities rather than for Thunder Bay and Sudbury which, once again, have better modes of transportation.

I can assure the minister that I am familiar with those routes in northern Ontario that he talks about, and this is not a question of servicing nine remote routes. Those areas that are serviced by the CN route can be serviced by other transportation modes at less expense.
I return to the question. Is it more important to service

Once again, people will continue to use the other modes of transportation. In the mean time, we have to serve all Canadians. Very honestly, that is what we tried to do in the decision we made last week.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare and it concerns pollution in the Great Lakes system. When the minister responded to my leader a few minutes ago, he said that since this government was elected in 1984 it had acted on pollution.

closed, the wildlife interpretation centre was closed, and the Great Lakes pollution monitoring program was eliminated. There was an exhaustive report on pollution which came out of National Health and Welfare. That report was killed by the Department of the Environment.
