He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak on the motion for second reading of
Bill C-28, which implements the changes to the Income Tax Act announced in the April Budget of the Minister of Finance.

Some fiscal measures have already been presented in this House. Bill C-17 was referred to a committee after receiving concise but thorough consideration during second reading. I trust this Bill will receive the same efficient consideration.

This is not the first budget bill to be discussed by this House as a result of the April budget. Bill C-17, which amends the Customs Tariff Act, received concise but thorough consideration at all stages in this House, I am happy to note, and Bill C-20 amending the Excise Tax is in committee for study. I trust this bill will receive the same efficient consideration as those bills did.

I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the measures in the bill now before us have to be seen clearly in the overall context of the budget's goals. As the Minister of Finance stated in his budget, Canada's large and growing debt is a serious problem that must be brought under control so that we can build for the future, not borrow from it. The measures in Bill C-28 make a major contribution to achieving that goal.
I want to be very precise about what I mean by controlling the debt, and about the measures that will contribute to it. Controlling the debt is not an end in itself. It is a means to an end-an essential precondition to the maintenance of our social and other programs, and to the achievement of sustained economic growth, improved competitiveness and the creation of productive jobs.

I believe, Mr. Speaker, that every member of this House shares with this government the desire to reach these goals. We all want an environment in which inflation and interest rates can come down. That means we must have firm, measured and consistent fiscal and monetary policies. Reducing the deficit and controlling the debt are an integral part of our policy approach. The April budget responds to the need for fiscal action to control the debt. It contains a balanced package of measures that places the greater burden on those who are better able to bear it.
October 11, 1989

On the spending side, our government has made expenditure cuts in areas such as defence, foreign aid, business subsidies and other transfers, payments to Crown corporations and government operations. These are effective in the current year and will have a substantial impact on spending for several years into the future.
These expenditure control measures, together with the revenue measures in the budget, will reduce the deficit by over $5 billion this year and $9 billion next year. This year they will almost offset the rise in interest costs and leave a deficit of $30.5 billion. Next year the deficit is projected to drop to $28 billion and in five years time it will be cut in half.
I want to turn now to the revenue measures of the budget and, more specifically, to review the measures specifically and directly related to the Income Tax Act.

With regard to changes made to the personal income tax and the tax itself, Bill C-28 implements an increase in the personal surtax, which will rise from 3 per cent to 5 per cent. As well, an additional high-income surtax of 3 per cent will be applied to federal income tax on income in excess of $15,000. These measures will be phased in over two years, and will be fully applied in taxation year 1990. In 1989 the effect will be that the basic personal surtax will be increased to 4 per cent and the high-income surtax will be effective at a rate of 1.5 per cent.
While acting to bring the public debt under control, the government has examined the tax base to ensure that no Canadian bears a disproportionate level of income tax. This Bill, consequently, includes measures to improve the fairness of the tax base.
Specifically, the Bill introduces taxation of accrued investment income on a annual basis. In this way, taxpayers who invest in contracts which pay interest annually and those who choose to invest in compound instruments will be taxed on a comparable basis.

Measures are also introduced to ensure that lessors of property must recognize leasing profits on a current basis. This enables the government to ensure that the leasing industry bears its fair share of tax and curtails the use of leasing as an after-tax financing mechanism.
Government Orders
While these new measures will limit the tax advantages of leasing property, they will not affect the other desirable attributes of leasing. In particular, these measures will allow those people who lease property to claim capital cost allowance as if they had acquired the property directly.
The personal income tax system plays a major role in managing the over-all spending of the government. It does this by providing a basis for income tested assistance and by providing for taxation at progressive rates of most types of government assistance received by individuals. This role is being expanded by measures in Bill C-28.
These amendments provide for the recovery of various types of federal social assistance from those taxpayers who do not need assistance from the government. By moving to a more progressive system, the government is ensuring the continued existence of these programs for taxpayers who need help. By assuring the continued viability of these social programs, this bill is making an extremely important contribution to the maintenance of our social safety net.

The budget also included significant measures relating to changes made to the corporate tax system. We believe it is important to ensure that all large corporations pay tax and contribute to debt control. Therefore, effective July 1 of this year, a tax on large corporations was introduced. This tax, which will be levied at a rate of 0.175 per cent on capital employed in Canada in excess of $10 million, will ensure that all large companies pay federal taxes and thus contribute to debt reduction.
We expect that some 3,600 corporations which account for approximately three-quarters of total corporate capital employed in Canada, will be subject to the tax. Together with modifications to the existing corporate surtax, this measure is expected to raise $965 million in additional federal revenue in its first full year of application.

This bill also contains a number of measures dealing with securities lending and dividend rental arrangements. These measures are designed to facilitate the efficient operation of Canada's capital markets while

October 11, 1989
Government Orders
eliminating the revenue loss arising from certain tax motivated dividend rental arrangements.
The new rules ensure that a securities loan will not be regarded as a disposition of the security and will therefore not give rise to gains or losses for tax purposes. They provide that the lender of a share will be entitled to trade compensatory payments received from the borrower of the share as dividends. To offset the cost of these benefits such payments will be non-deductible to the borrowers.
However, where a person borrows shares only to take advantage of the favourable tax treatment afforded any dividends paid on the shares while they are borrowed, the borrower will now be considered to have entered into a dividend rental arrangement. The borrower will therefore be denied the dividend tax credit or inter-corporate dividend deduction, whichever is applicable.
This legislation recognizes the importance of securities lending in the operation of Canada's capital markets. It will provide greater certainty of tax treatment for investors and securities dealers alike. Together, these measures will facilitate legitimate securities lending but will curtail share lending only for tax purposes.

Finally, as a result of ongoing consultations with the securities industry, the deduction for dividend compensation payments for all taxpayers will be disallowed, effective July 1, 1989. In the case of payments made by registered securities dealers, the disallowance will be phased in so that only one third of such payments made before April 1, 1990 will be non-deductible.
Accordingly, the 50 per cent phase-in for the disallowance of dividend compensation payments, announced in the May 26 press release from the Department of Finance, will not be implemented. We will monitor the impact of these new rules to ensure that the Canadian securities industry maintains its international competitiveness.

The government has not forgotten how important it is to ensure that persons who owe income tax actually pay that tax. To encourage taxpayers to pay their taxes on a
timely basis, this bill will increase the rate of interest payable on overdue tax payments by two percentage points. A similar increase will be made to the rate of interest paid by the government on overdue refunds. There are also provisions to ensure that corporate tax payments due to the government are delivered on time.
An underlying principle of our government's economic policies is fairness and compassion for all Canadians. This must be reflected in the tax system. A number of measures in Bill C-28 are intended to assist certain categories of taxpayers who deserve further help.

Accordingly the Bill provides for:
-new deductions in respect of part-time attendant care expenses for the working disabled,
-the deduction of certain legal expenses incurred to obtain a pension benefit or retiring allowance,
-an expanded list of medical expenses qualifying for tax assistance, to include eight new medical devices, and
-other amendments to ensure that certain counselling benefits provided to employees are not taxable.
Bill C-28 also introduces a new drought relief tax deferral in respect of cattle farmers who have had to reduce the size of their breeding herds as a result of drought. These measures all improve the fairness of the tax system, and will assist those Canadians who face difficulties not encountered by most of their fellow citizens.
In conclusion, the measures in this bill have benefited from extensive consultations with taxpayers and their advisors. It is very important that this legislation be passed as quickly as possible, to remove the uncertainty that inevitably exists for the very large number of taxpayers, both individuals and businesses, affected by these amendments.

As members of the House, we must all realize that the seriousness of Canada's debt problem requires equally serious determination and action on the part of the government to bring it under control. Acting now will

enable us to maintain and protect social and other programs for Canadians today as well as in the future.
In addition, acting now will give us the fiscal flexibility in the future to respond to the priorities that Canadians feel strongly about. That is our objective.
The measures in this bill, together with the other measures in the budget, will help us deal with the debt problem in the interest of all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the minister carefully and not once did I hear him mention our old age pensioners who are being brutally attacked in this bill.
This bill is an attack on the rights of our senior citizens. It is an attack on old age pensions. This bill is an attack on the rights of children. This bill is an attack on family allowances. This bill is an attack on the principle of universality of our social programs. This bill is an attack on the social contract that has governed this country for the 20th century. This bill is a betrayal of the promises of the Prime Minister of Canada. This bill is a betrayal of what the Prime Minister once called "a sacred trust".
Hear, hear!

This bill makes 59 amendments to the Income Tax Act. No one can deal with all of them in the time allowed within the rules. I cannot deal with all of them. I just want to mention one other briefly, and then I am going to document the treachery and deception of this government in its dealings with Canadian families and with our senior citizens.

First of all I would like to talk about the special income surtax the Government introduced in 1986. Members will recall that the Minister of Finance referred to this surtax as a temporary one when he announced it here in the House. According to the Minister, it would not be in effect for very long. The 1987 Budget clearly indicated that the tax would be eliminated as soon as the new sales tax came into force. The Minister of Finance said at the time that:
As soon as the new tax became effective, surtaxes on personal and
corporate income would be abolished.
Government Orders
That is what he said, Mr. Speaker, and that is what he promised. But what did he actually do? The surtaxes are still with us. In fact, they have increased from 3 per cent to 5 per cent for middle-income Canadians and up to 8 per cent for Canadians on high incomes, and they are no longer temporary but permanent. They are now an integral part of the Canadian tax system. The Minister's technical paper on the goods and services tax does not say the surtaxes will be eliminated. These new surtaxes against individuals, surtaxes that are no longer temporary by permanent, will cost Canadians $1.1 billion more, which is a flagrant contradiction of the Government's stated objectives of its tax reform. According to the Minister, the main purpose of tax reform was to reduce personal income tax.

So much for this minister's idea of tax reform because it has proven to be nothing but a sham. It is nothing but a disguised tax increase, nothing but a massive tax grab under the umbrella of so-called reform. With this government there has been nothing but increase after increase ever since it was sworn into office. Since 1984 they have increased taxes 31 times.
I want to deal now in more detail with the so-called claw-back provisions on family allowances and old age pensions contained in this bill. I am not surprised that the minister in his presentation before the House ignored it. This claw-back is the culmination of years of deception-years of deception by this Prime Minister and by this Minister of Finance, deception of their true intentions with regard to the universality of our social programs. This government and this Prime Minister has consistently misled Canadians.
Listen to what the Prime Minister himself said in 1984. "Social programs were"-and I repeat those words: "-a sacred trust never to be tampered with".
Shortly after his election he tried to deindex the old age pension. He and the Minister of Finance backed down, but only after an enormous public outcry, an outcry backed by members of Parliament from this side of the House. We forced them back because they had broken their promise, they had broken that sacred trust.
Hear, hear!

One would have thought, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister of this country would have learned a lesson. But there he was again in 1988 in another election, this time using his mother as a prop. He was on stage with his own mother saying that he would never do anything to reduce social

October 11, 1989
Government Orders
programs. He repeated to the country the promise of a sacred trust. Indeed, on October 15, 1988, during the election campaign in Summerside, Prince Edward Island-and that is one community he never should dare to visit again-
Hear, hear!

-the Prime Minister said to the people of Summerside, and through them to the people of Prince Edward Island and Atlantic Canada, the following: "As long as I am Prime Minister of Canada, social benefits, especially those for the elderly, will be improved, not diminished by our government". What could be more categorical? What could be less ambiguous? What could be a more definitive commitment to the senior citizens of our country than that statement made a few weeks before the election in 1988?

Mr. Speaker, I had the privilege of taking part in two national debates, one in English and one in French. I have here a copy of the transcript of the French debate, including a question put by reporter Daniel Lessard. This is what Mr. Lessard said in front of the camera, in front of a national audience, in French: "Mr. Mulroney, are you ready this evening to promise, before Madame Denis and before all Canadians, not to touch senior citizens' pensions and to maintain, in their entirety, our social programs?"
Mr. Speaker, I may remind you that Madame Denis is the same Madame Solange Denis who came here on Parliament Hill and told Mr. Mulroney, to his face: "Mr. Mulroney, you lied, you betrayed us. At the next election it will be: Goodbye, Charlie Brown, we won't forget that!" And Madame Denis was right!
And here is Mr. Mulroney's answer in French to Mr. Lessard: , "As far as the future is concerned, I find that our system which we have in place is sound and deserves to be respected and maintained".

Because we are being listened to in both languages and because that commitment was so categorical, Mr. Speaker, I am sure you will excuse my translating that, repeating it in our other official language.
This was a question put to the Prime Minister of Canada in the national debate in French during the last federal election campaign. It was a debate in which the member for Oshawa, Mr. Broadbent, the Prime Minister, Mr. Mulroney, and I engaged the attention of Canadians. It was put by Daniel Lessard, one of the three journalists asking questions of us.
Mr. Lessard asked the Prime Minister this question: "Are you ready this evening to promise before Madame Solange Denis, and before all Canadians, not to touch senior citizens' pensions and to maintain, in their entirety, our social programs?" The Prime Minister responded and I quote: "As far as the future is concerned, I find that the system which we have in place is sound and deserves to be respected and maintained".
That was the Prime Minister's commitment to Canadians during the French language debate. That was the ultimate in deception towards our senior citizens. That was the ultimate in political fraud.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, that 1988 commitment was worth as little as the commitment made by the Prime Minister in 1984. It was just part of the deceptive strategy for getting re-elected. It is no wonder while we sit in this House of Commons-elected by the people of Canada-that public cynicism is at an all-time high. It is no wonder that those of us in public life do not receive from our fellow citizens the credit that sometimes we feel we deserve. People do not know whom to trust anymore. If they cannot trust the Prime Minister, whom can they trust in the public life of our country?
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, there has been deception after deception. The Prime Minister's word meant absolutely nothing. The bill before this House proves that without a doubt.

When we on this side of the House warned senior citizens they could not trust this government, this is what the Minister of Finance had to say during that same election campaign. I quote his remarks made in St. John's, Newfoundland as reported by The Evening Telegram on November 2, 1988:
I say to Ed Broadbent and I say to John Uirner, don't go into the old age homes in this country and frighten widows and widowers who are 80, 85 and 90 years old with things that are patently untrue. Try to fight the election on the facts. Playing on the fears and emotions of some of the most defenceless people in our society today is despicable. If you want to pick on Brian Mulroney, if you want to pick on Mike Wilson, that's fine, that's politics. But don't pick on our senior citizens.
Who is picking on our senior citizens now? Who is attacking their pensions? Not me, Mr. Speaker. It is the government opposite. It is doing exactly what we thought it would do. It is doing exactly what we said it would do, and worse.
Before the Empire Club the Minister of Finance, talking about the sales tax and replying to me when I said it would cost Canadians billions of dollars more-and it is-called me a coward and a liar. He said there would not be one additional cent of tax. That is the type of rhetoric, the type of morality we are dealing with.
If you allow me a little peripheral, but germane, comment to the subject of taxation, Mr. Speaker, for five years I have listened to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance attempt to misrepresent my record as Minister of Finance. I can look at that gentleman over there who holds the custodianship now, the fiduciary responsibility, for the finances of the country. I was the last Minister of Finance to present a surplus to this country and to this House of Commons in 1973, two successive surpluses, and in five budgets an annual deficit on average of $710 million-not $30 billion-plus as we have.had for the last five years. I have been listening to this for five years.
I would like to take a few minutes to tell the House what I did, under the leadership of Mr. Trudeau, for senior citizens as minister of finance compared with what this government and this minister are doing. The rhetoric of this government and of the Prime Minister is good but rhetoric does not do anything to put money into the
Government Orders
pockets and purses of our senior citizens. You will forgive me, Your Honour, if this sounds moderately immodest, but the facts speak for themselves. With Mr. Trudeau's complete backing I indexed the old age security pension to the cost of living to protect our senior citizens completely from inflation.
Hear, hear!

I told this House of Commons that I did not want to see the men and women of this country who had contributed a lifetime of their earnings, their savings, their productivity and their energy to building this country when they had retired and could no longer protect themselves from inflation, bear the brunt of it. I said that the country will protect you, and will protect you absolutely. That is what we did.
Hear, hear!

The current Minister of Finance, again with the complete backing of his Prime Minister, is withdrawing that protection from our senior citizens. I increased the old age pension, first by 11 per cent. I increased the tax exemption for senior citizens by 54 per cent.

Hear, hear!
Mr Turner (Vancouver Quadra): Again, with Mr. Trudeau's backing, I increased the basic old age pension by another 21 per cent. Once more with the backing of the Prime Minister of the day I cut taxes by 8 per cent and indexed the Canada pension plan.
Yes, it is true that in 1972 and 19741 made promises to the senior citizens of this country. The difference between me and the current Minister of Finance is I kept my promises and this minister broke his.
Hear, hear!

Never once as minister of finance, never once during the difficult times of the world-wide oil crisis in 1973-74, did I reduce any of our benefits to our senior citizens, because in the Liberal Party we have always believed that we honour our elders, we honour our senior citizens, we do not attack their basic rights.

Mr. Speaker, if this Bill is passed, and they have a majority, old age pensions and family allowances will no

October 11, 1989
Government Orders
longer be universal. The Government is not only changing the foundation of these programs, it is creating precedents that will affect other social programs.
The Bill before the House today creates special measures to tax the old age pensions and family allowances of people with incomes of $50,000 or more. The cut-off point of $50,000 is only partly indexed, because there is no compensation for inflation over 3 per cent. The cut-off point will not follow annual inflation, so that in real terms, it will go down. Ten years from now, nearly one million Canadian families will lose all or part of their family allowances and old age pensions.

The minister and the Prime Minister say that the programs are still universal because everybody still gets a cheque. What they are not admitting is that along with the pension cheque or the family allowance cheque, they are also sending out a tax invoice at the same time to certain Canadians based on income. They are saying it is universal unless you make x amount of dollars per year.
There is one honest member of Parliament on the government side. He may be out of control. He may be a loose cannon. He may be a one-man fog-horn from coast to coast, but I will say this for the hon. member for Mississauga South, he may from time to time bring the good reputation of this House into question, but at least he speaks the truth.
This is a letter that he wrote in response to a constituent of his. I do not know whether any of you ever received a response from the member for Mississauga South, but this one is a collector's item. He does reply to his constituents. The senior citizen is obviously complaining about the claw-back on his old age pension. This appears as reported in The Ottawa Citizen on September 23. The headline is: "MP contradicts PM over 'sacred trust' These are the words of the member for Mississauga South:
With respect to your claw-back matter, I understand your
concern.
How about that? That is unusually sensitive for this particular member.
This is what he wrote in response to a letter of complaint written by 61-year old William Daly.
We have decided to eliminate universality and we do that in a sense by the claw-back in both family allowance and the old age pension.
As you know, it has been a Conservative philosophy for some time that distributions from the state ought to go essentially to those in need. While the claw-back may be unfair and sneaky, it is there.
That unmasks it all. I do not question the sincerity of the minister who appeared this afternoon. I do not blame him for not mentioning it because why defend the indefensible? Why defend something that would enrage every senior citizen in this country who is now watching the House of Commons?
It is not universal, Mr. Speaker. Let us face it. We are back to the old means test. We now have an income tested program. That is what this debate is all about.
What is more, people will be taxed differently depending on where their income comes from. A senior who receives pension income will pay more tax than another senior whose income comes primarily from investments.
Single-earner families will be discriminated against. If both parents work and they earn $49,000 each for a total family income of $98,000, there is no claw-back in the family allowance or pension. But if it is a one-earner family with an income over $50,000 they lose benefits. That is not only not fair, it is stupid.
I now wish to address social contracts. When the old age pension was introduced, a special tax was created to help pay for it. I want to quote from the 1971 tax guide, and this also appeared in earlier tax guides since the installation of the old age pension. Canadians who paid tax in the early 1950s until 1971 paid a special surtax. The 1971 tax guide states: "All taxpayers whose taxable income is over $500 are subject to the Old Age Security Ikx. The tax is 4 per cent of taxable income-maximum $240."
This tax was in effect until 1971. Canadians who paid that tax throughout the 1950s and 1960s until 1971, and that includes almost everybody over the age of 40 including those receiving pensions today, are now to be deprived of the benefits of what they believed that tax was earning them. That is nothing short of straight robbery. They paid the tax for the pension and, unilaterally, without any advance notice they are being deprived of the pension which that tax earned them.
October 11, 1989

Those senior citizens who contributed 4 per cent of their income on a special tax in the 1950s and 1960s and will now have 100 per cent of their pension clawed back, taxed back, in effect are paying a tax of 104 per cent. They paid thousands of dollars over a 20-year period believing that they were going to be entitled to the full old age pension. Now it has been taken from them. That is expropriation without compensation. The senior citizens of this country will demand compensation at the next general election.
Hear, hear!

This is abandonment of the commitments and the social contracts that governments have had with the people in this country. What this government is saying to Canadians is "Don't count on it. Don't count on having a pension when you reach retirement age. Don't count on having a family allowance when you are trying to raise a family because we could rejig these numbers next week, next month, next year, or in three years." Once a government decides to set a discretionary limit on the total amount of the pension, whether it is $50,000 today or $40,000 tomorrow, nobody is safe and nobody can count on it because it is no longer a right of citizenship, it depends on the pure, unadulterated, unilateral discretion of the government of the day.

What about the social contract? What about the government's commitment to maintain its part of the contract? The Prime Minister has forgotten about it. The Minister of Finance has reneged on the contract. The Government simply does not believe in the universality of social programs. Why not admit it? Why not come out and say so? Why not? Because if they admit that universality no longer has its place in our country, the government denies what it has repeated and promised over and over again. It prefers to end universality in a roundabout way. Canadians, however, are not easily fooled.

Don't take it just from me. The National Council on Welfare had this to say: "The move away from universal benefits is the most significant change in social policy in a generation. Yet it was announced by the Minister of Finance in a budget speech with no prior consultation. In
Government Orders
the case of seniors, the federal government had publicly rejected the idea of a clawback or a surtax on old age pensions as late as January, 1985, on the grounds that it would seriously disrupt the retirement income system. The clawback changes the rules of the game without their consent. The elderly have already paid for their old age pensions through a lifetime of paying income taxes."
That was a press release by the council on September 13,1989. The president of the Senior Citizens Federation says the following in a letter dated June 23, 1989, to the Prime Minister: "We view this proposal as a serious breach of faith by our government and an insidious effort to undercut the social security programs that you have on numerous times stated are a sacred trust."
In a letter dated May 24, 1989 to the Minister of Finance the Coalition of Quebec Seniors says: "The pension clawback is discriminatory on the basis of age, unfair, and contrary to the Charter of Rights. It creates a steeper tax rate for seniors than for others of similar income levels. Seniors who with great difficulty have succeeded over the years in saving for their retirement are being penalized".
What this proposal means, of course, is that a senior with an income of $70,000 per year will be taxed differently than someone younger making the same amount of money. That is not fair and it doesn't make sense.
Why from this comer of the House, both in this House and across the country, certainly since the days of Mackenzie King, and then on to Mr. St. Laurent, Mr. Pearson, Mr. Trudeau, have we always believed in universality? Why has universality been the guiding principle in the social programs accepted in this country? We have tried to explain this principle to the government. This government has never been able to grasp it. I will try again.
If there is one characteristic that is Canadian, if there is one quality by which we like to define ourselves, it is the quality of fairness, equal opportunity and equal treatment. We believe that no matter where you come from, where you live, what you earn, who your family is that you have an equal right to the social programs of this country, that all individuals are entitled to the social programs as a right of citizenship. It is part of the social

Government Orders
contract in return for a lifetime of contribution to our community.
We believe that all Canadians deserve that equal and equitable treatment no matter what their social status. Universality means that everyone is treated the same. We do not mean that you don't tax the rich more than the poor. We believe in a progressive income tax where those who have the ability to pay, pay. That is the fault with this goods and services tax. It is regressive.
We have always believed that if you limit programs and direct them to the poor, if you design them for the poor, if you design them for those at the lower income scales, then those programs inevitably become poor programs. Universality means that the rich man and the poor man wait in the same doctor's office for the same service and are covered in the same way. They mean that regardless of income, regardless of connections, there is equal treatment.
Universality has been a unifying force in our country. It makes our social programs credible because there is no ghettoizing of the haves and the have-nots, such as the poor get something and the rich don't. Everybody does, subject to an over-all taxation system, but the programs are credible because when they come to all of us then we are all behind them. They are community programs, and that is why Canada has been the most successful country in the world.
Hear, hear!

The danger is that once you start tinkering with that principle, once you start undermining the principle of universality, you put everything in question. Who decides who gets what benefits? Where do you draw the line? Who decides which of our citizens need more help than the next one? Once the principle is abandoned and discretion is reintroduced into our social programs, what is next? Medicare? Hospitalization? Free public education? Oh, some members may raise their eyebrows, but this is the first government in Canadian history that has ever put a tax on learning, a tax on books. This government is destabilizing and endangering the social contract which is based on trust, legitimate expectation, reliance on the word of our public officers.
I hesitate to say, "I told you so". It is the worst thing you can say to a member of your family, the worst thing
you can say to a neighbour. You never get any credit for it. But I made a prediction in this House of Commons in December, 1984, when I spoke out against the government's proposal to de-index the Old Age Pension. I said then that this debate would not end until there was "a clear, unmistakable, credible, believable and unassailable commitment that the government will not tamper with the universality of the social programs of this country which are counted on by millions of Canadians. They are part of the social contract, part of the glue, the adhesion, and the unity that have made this country a very decent place to live". That is what I said then, and I regret that that prediction has come true.
I want to say to you, Sir, my colleagues will be entering this debate. This is not going to be the end of it. It is only, perhaps to use the Churchillian phrase, "the end of the beginning". Now we know. Now we have the legislation. It is before the House. Now we know that all those commitments made by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, those commitments to protect and defend and enhance our social programs, promises are not worth a damn. Now we know that this government has no commitment that cannot be broken, no matter how solemn the occasion, no matter how frequently it is made. That is the measure of this Prime Minister and this Minister of Finance, and that is the measure of this debate.
I could not be more serious when I say now we are dealing with part of the basic moral fibre and structure of this country. Can our politicians and public figures be trusted? If commitments of the Prime Minister made on several occasions on national television and across the country, not only in two federal elections, but whenever he was accosted by members of the public are no longer sacred-and now we know they are not-then on this side of the House on behalf of Canadians on this and other issues we are in a battle and we will press it right to the limit.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, the government would like to advise the House that tomorrow will be designated as an opposition day.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate my hon. colleague, the Leader of the Opposition, for his excellent speech.
I am honoured to lead off my party's debate on Bill C-28. I was going to say that it was a beautiful autumn day, resplendent in beautiful colours, with mother nature at work, a kaleidoscope and all of those beautiful terms, but really it is a black Wednesday in October across Canada. It is probably very appropriately a grim, sombre day because the discussion of Bill C-28 is an historic piece of legislation that spells the end of universality for social programs in Canada. A sacred trust of the Canadian people.
This government has created a new vernacular of political jargon in this country. Words such as reprofile, deregulate, privatize, rationalize, patronize, Americanize and finally benefit reduction tax, better known as the clawback. The name speaks for itself. This is on the heels of VIA cuts with the statement of the Prime Minister, "We must cut VIA in order to save it", and "We must decrease social benefits in order to maintain them". What sort of bizarre, fallacious reasoning in this? It is obviously Tory reasoning. It would earn a failure in logic in first-year university in philosophy and in the real world it is pure debauchery. This, indeed, is historic legislation, but history will not treat either legislation or the government kindly for its actions.
Speaking of history, I would like to cite some references dated, but nevertheless prophetic. William H. Seward, a Republican-no surprise-in January 1861 stated:
So I look upon Prince Rupert's Land and Canada, and saw how an ingenious people and a capable, enlightened government, are occupied with bridging rivers and making railroads and telegraphs to develop, organize and create and preserve the great British Provinces of the north; by the Great Lakes, the St. Lawrence and around the shores of Hudson's Bay, and I am able to say, "It is very well; you are building excellent states to be hereafter admitted to the American Union.
This government wants us to be like the United States. This legislation strikes out at the supposed richer, older citizens of our country. You know the now famous quote, Mr. Speaker: "As long as I am Prime Minister of Canada, social benefits will be improved, not diminished by this government which is committed to social justice and
Government Orders
fairness for all Canadians". He forgot to add, "fairness for all, except for children and senior citizens".
This was said in October 1988. What a dramatic turnabout, but a turnabout that we have grown all too used to.
Remember the free trade debate? Free trade will not affect our social programs. It will, in fact, enhance them. Some of the candidates brought out their mothers and fathers and said: "I would never deceive you. I would never lie to you. Please believe me, because my mother knows that I am telling the truth". Well, today every grandmother and grandfather in this country is getting a swift kick.
I do not accept the remarks of the finance committee chairman that older people don't wear out their clothes, or they don't buy furniture. The intimation is that older people are sedentary. They are not. This clawback is causing older citizens to rise up again and glut their ire as they did in 1984.
The problem with this legislation is that it is sneaky, pernicious, discriminatory, an attack on seniors, but is also a lever into attacking all of the social services that will affect 128,000 pensioners in 1990, but one million in 20 years from now. Let us remember that we are an aging population. The claws of clawback will eventually hit everybody if, God forbid, this government remains in power.
We are not only talking to 65 year olds, but we are talking to 25 year olds making $25,000 now, with salary increased only by inflation. They will have part of their Old Age Security clawed back at retirement. So we are are not just talking about 65 year olds, we are talking about 25 year olds, 35 year olds, and 45 year olds.
What do seniors think? Not that the government cares. An editorial from The Legion magazine of July and August, 1989, put it very succinctly: "Indeed, even if the $50,000 income threshold will drop in real terms because it will not be indexed to a level of inflation, but only to inflation minus 3 per cent, with a reduction of the real income at which the tax kicks in, more seniors will have to pay more money. Not coincidentally the numbers of seniors will be increasing as Canada's population ages collectively. In more than just a decade, a large number of seniors will be caught in the net and it won't be just the big fish. In essence, the government is sneaking up

October 11, 1989
Government Orders
on us. What we have here, in addition to the government's betrayal of public trust, is a case of age discrimination".
Up to this point I have spoken in generalities. Many people will say: "Well, it doesn't apply to me". I want to cite a specific case of a constituent of mine who came into the office and talked about this clawback. She was fighting mad, upset, hurt, and indignant. Her story, we cannot generalize that just because someone makes $50,000 a year that means one is well to do and can easily afford to give back some of one's Old Age Security. This lady is a single woman. She worked for 35 to 40 years in a well-paid responsible position. She was a very budget conscious person for all of her working life. At retirement she had placed $250,000 into the provincial and federal tax coffers. The 1971 tax guideline, clause 37, Section 3, Old Age Security Act states: "All taxpayers whose taxable income is over $500 are subject to the old age security tax. The tax is 4 per cent of taxable income."
This lady lives in a non-profit housing unit. Her rent has gone from $426 to $469 to $510 per month in the last 15 months. The 4 per cent rent guideline does not apply to non-profit housing. Because of this woman's good fortune she has set up a $10,000 scholarship for a needy student. Excellent. Now she finds out that the company she worked for for 35 or 40 years has been bought out by another larger company and her pension is on hold. She has worked all of this out for 35 to 40 years and the whole budget is now shot. In tears she states that there is a lifelong budget shot to hell.
There are many stories out there similar to this. Different circumstances but, nevertheless, there can be a tragic end. Universality is not a right of citizenship any more. You will be asked: "Do you deserve it? Do you need it? Do you qualify for it? Prove it". If only big business had the same kind of morals.
Going back to free trade. The end of universality is a government desire. We want to be like the United States. I cite the problems since January 1 of harassment by Americans regarding pork, lumber, fish, and steel. Subsidies were supposed to be negotiated over the next seven years. Yet when a punitive duty was brought against Sysco and Algoma Steel the Minister for International Trade said: "Oh, well, everyone knows that Sysco is highly subsidized". So, they are now a write-off.
I wrote letters to the Prime Minister and the Minister for International Trade with regard to this punitive duty against the steel mill in my city. I got no response nor any reaction whatsoever. The free trade agreement binds us, it permeates all of our discussions, and makes us more and more like the United States.
A reputable politician, Mr. Gotlieb, the ex-Canadian ambassador to the United States states: "Lobbying in the United States is now vital. The free trade agreement offered us no protection whatsoever. We have to get in there and lobby for our rights". We should take his advice. It is important.
Social programs are no longer a sacred cow. The cow will soon be dead and the bleeding has begun. The end of universality has begun and it is acknowledged by the government's finance committee chairman. I will cite the same letter. We have a copy of the letter if one would deny the report of the Ottawa Citizen. I think it bears repeating. As you know, it has been a conservative philosophy for some time that distributions from the state ought to go essentially to those in need. While the clawback may be unfair and sneaky it is there. That says it all. That really does say it all.
The National Council on Welfare report is financed by the government and has various points with regard to the illegitimacy of the clawback. I would like to highlight number seven. "The clawback could erode support for social programs. Eventually it will weaken popular support for social programs in general including those which help the poor. Giving benefits with one hand and taking them all back with the other is a hypocritical policy that could engender middle-income voters' resentment at paying taxes for social programs to which they are not really entitled". In layman's terms people will say: "Well, I don't want to pay into it because I am not going to receive anything from it".
Time will not permit me to elaborate on the family allowance clawback but it is, suffice it to say, that the same scenario will evolve and within ten years 30 per cent of all families will be negatively affected.
This legislation hits everybody. It hits the seniors, it hits young people, but of course it hits the middle-income group that has to support these young people. As far as transfer payments are concerned, they are being cut in this omnibus tax bill. Under Established Programs Financing the federal government provides support to the provinces in the form of cash and tax transfers for
October 11, 1989

health care and post-secondary education. In the Budget the government announced it would cut the growth in its EPF transfers by one percentage point beginning in 1990-91.
I should like to turn to one of my favourite books and I have read it perhaps a hundred times because I cannot believe what I read. It is called Where I Stand, by our Prime Minister. This was written when he was at his zenith of popularity. He is talking about research and development and he says:
The starling line for me is the technological dimension. Either we go into the game and become important players in this major league or we become a nation that will, during its entire lifetime, play in the Junior B circuit. To play with the majors, we must make a firm commitment to double the public and private funds allocated to research and development-Research and development, and the resulting innovations are the lifeblood of a successful economy and country.
And he goes on:
As a percentage of its population, Canada employs in research and development one-third as many people as do the Swedes, the Germans, and the Japanese and one-half as many as the Dutch, the French, and the Americans. Of all the industrialized countries of the Western world, Ireland and Iceland are the only countries that invest less than we do in this vital field.
We must double our research and development. And part of that doubling has to come through transfer payments. Now that is the myth, this is the reality.
John Ferguson of Southam News writes:
Meanwhile, indications are that total spending on research and development in which we already lag far behind our major trading partners appears to have declined again last year as a proportion of the economy.
Mulroney promised in the 1984 election that Canada would double spending on R and D under a Tory government. It was then 1.37 per cent of gross domestic product. It slid to 1.31 per cent in 1987 and when the 1988 figures come out they will likely show the figure below 1.30 per cent.
In the same article Mr. Ferguson writes:
Another sign of waning interest: the 34-member National Advisory Committee on Science and Technology, chaired by Mulroney and touted as a signal of his commitment, has not met since last summer.
Government Orders
How can we do better when we cut, cut, cut? All of these measures will condemn us to be hewers of wood and drawers of water in perpetuity. Transfer payments affect our post-secondary education and hospital care. This could create two tiers of medical care, one for the have-provinces and one for the have-not provinces. The Canadian Medical Association says: "We are headed toward a two-tier health care system with one quality of health care in the rich provinces and second or third-rate services in the poor provinces".
Today I received a fax from Sault Ste. Marie in Ontario, which is one of the have-provinces and perhaps no one would deny that we in Ontario are indeed fortunate. But, the health care system in Ontario is in disarray, operated by a Liberal government, handling what meagre funds the Tory government passes on to it. This report is extremely upsetting, to say the least. A local individual perhaps lost his life because one of the best hospitals in Ontario could not care for him. It did not have the staff available. This is an indication that when the have-provinces are having problems, you can see what reduction in transfer payments could result in.
As far as the system is concerned, the system will work for those who are in the system who can play the system, but most average Canadians have no idea what the system is or how they can participate. The indication that average Canadians have been consulted on this tax bill, are, of course, erroneous.
James Carter said in 1895: "In every community those who feel the burdens of taxation are naturally prone to relieve themselves from it if they can. One class struggles to throw the burden off its shoulders. If they succeed, of course, it must fall upon others. They also in turn labour to get rid of it. Finally, the load falls upon those who will not or cannot make a successful effort for relief. This is in general a one-sided struggle in which the rich only engage and which the poor always go to the wall".
This legislation is a natural fallout from the budget. Let there be no doubt that this was a big business budget. When they brought forth all of their wishes from the wish book they got just about what they wanted.
Their wish list contained the following: the government must set targets for reducing the deficit and sustain the effort over a number of years of unshakeable

Government Orders
commitment; the deficit must be slated to fall by close to $7 billion per year; expenditure reduction should make up the bulk of cuts in the deficit. The following recommendation is particularly noteworthy: since social programs make up 60 per cent of government program spending, social programs should be the major target.
It is coming true. They say that any social program spending should be targeted only to those in need. This means the end to any concept of universality, including universal pensions. Tax increases will have to form some part of the deficit reduction strategy. Such tax hikes should be temporary when possible and applied to deficit reduction. The manufacturers' sales tax should be replaced with a national sales tax, and the federal government should introduce this unilaterally if it cannot secure provincial support. Small business groups caution that sales tax reform should be done very carefully if they are to support it. Ideally the tax should have no exemptions or exceptions and regressivity should be offset for the poor by a refundable tax credit.
Everything they wanted they got. Business should not be exempt from the program cuts to carry its share of the burden. Expenditure cuts to business should look at limiting industrial grants and subsidies for regional development. These were recommendations by the big business lobby.
I say that this big business lobby has become very sophisticated in its public relations. They say: "We have to tread softly not to upset the average Canadians. Let us put this kind of rhetoric in here and we will deceive them." Indeed I think people were deceived at first, but now they are starting to catch on and people are upset. They are extremely upset with the whole budgeting process and the tax grab by this government.
Since taxation is complicated and there are many different taxes involved, the ordinary citizen might be forgiven for being a bit confused. But if a large majority of Canadians have felt in the past that the rich were not paying enough tax, once the smoke and mirrors of the current reform are removed these same Canadians may be surprised to find that the rich are paying even less tax.
The finance minister's tax reform or tax deform, depending on how you take it, is indeed mostly smoke and mirrors. There is a lot of talk about making the rich pay more and helping those at the bottom end of the economy. In reality the reforms do almost nothing to achieve those ends. Some well-to-do investors in the corporations will pay more but most high rollers will pay less.
There was very little outcry. The Financial Post and The Financial Times, and The Globe's report on business, lost interest veiy, very quickly in the tax reform, indicating that it was a pleasant budget for big business.
The finance minister's reform has not really caused the government to veer from its agenda at all, except perhaps to throw out a quick tax reduction a few years ago. From the beginning the government has been moving toward a much heavier emphasis on the sales tax, the most regressive kind of tax. Since it came to power in 1984 it has increased corporate taxes by only 4.2 per cent while it increased income tax by 48.2 per cent.
I believe our party will soon be talking about implementing a wealth tax because the top 10 per cent in this country own more than half the country's wealth.
We are in step with the United States. Everything that we once stood for, revered, enjoyed, accepted and expected is being cut from under us. This is a very sorry day. These are sorry times. Until Canadians rise as one and shout: "we are as mad as hell, we are not going to put up with it any more"-and I think it is getting closer and closer-the government will move forward with its agenda, an agenda which is destroying us and making us a market driven, profit motivated society where only the fittest survive. What about the rest-and the rest-and the rest.
We beseech the government to rescind its clawback for the benefit of all Canadians. The Prime Minister said not too long ago: "We are in the process of building two Canadas-one which is rich and promising and one which is underdeveloped and underemployed", which is unacceptable. We agree whole-heartedly with the Prime Minister that this is totally unacceptable.
October 11, 1989

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to a major piece of legislation, Bill C-28, and especially to answer the former Minister of Finance of this country who, as you know Mr. Speaker, took us from being hard-pressed to depressed, and I am referring to the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner), the Leader of the Opposition.
Right on!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, strangely enough, not so long ago the Leader of the Opposition got rid of his financial critic because he said the Conservative government's policies were good. So he was kicked out. And I can predict, Mr. Speaker, that the regional president of the federal Liberal Party- The truth is never palatable, Mr. Speaker, but we all need to hear the truth from time to time.
That is not the truth!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Now what did I say, Mr. Speaker-
It didn't take us 20 years to see the light.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the courtesy to listen to my colleagues and I think they should do the same for me. They would learn something.
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, I can predict that the regional president of the federal Liberal party in our area will soon be on the outs, because only last week, he said he agreed with the economic policies of the Conservative Party in the riding of Trois-Rivieres. Just watch, Mr. Speaker: their regional president will soon be fired, just like their financial critic.
Talk about the bill, not the Liberal Party!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Be patient! We'll get there. Nothing to get excited about. We have the whole afternoon!
When I hear the former Minister of Finance, who at the time managed to increase the deficit very substantially, when I hear him talk about the elderly and the last budget, it reminds me of the economic statement of 1984, the budget of 1985, the budget of 1986, the budget of 1987 and the budget of 1988. That makes five, Mr. Speaker. The Leader of the Opposition must have taken the speeches he made on those occasions and used them to write the one he gave today. If he had given us a replay of his speeches on past Budgets, it would have
Government Orders
been the same speech, absolutely identical. The economy will be in bad shape. The elderly will be in bad shape, family allowances, and so forth- And this while our records show that 1.5 million jobs were created during the past four years in this country, permanent jobs, which means ten times as many as the previous Liberal government created over the same period, and that Government created part-time jobs, Mr. Speaker. And people remember that! Talk to the people in Trois-Rivieres and they will tell you all about it.
Mr. Speaker, just I am sure you do on the weekend, I make the rounds among the various senior citizens' clubs:	Sainte-Marguerite, Saint-Jean-de-Breboeuf,
Saint-Philippe and Radisson. During the budget period, they asked me: What's all this about old age security pensions and returning part of our cheque and so forth! I said: Listen, if you have a gross annual income of $77,000, not $42,000, not $24,000 and not $52,000 but $77,000, you will have to return part of your old age security pension. And you know what, Mr. Speaker? The people in the riding of Trois-Rivieres said: It's not a bad idea. The senior citizens in the riding of Trois-Rivieres said: It makes good sense.
If I have an annual income of $77,000,1 can give back part of my old age security cheque as tax to the federal government and I will still be able to live very well. That is what is in the Conservative government's 1989 budget. And I think that at some point, we must call a spade a spade. For 20 years, there was shameless waste by the former Liberal government, Mr. Speaker, so that when we took power in 1984, the accumulated debt was $200 billion and the annual deficit was $39 billion. It is funny how the Opposition does not talk when we speak the truth! It is funny how they become very quiet.
We must be realistic, Mr. Speaker. What has this government done for four years? It is true that we raised taxes, yes! I do not think there is a member on this side of the House who will not admit that. We will also admit something, Mr. Speaker: since tax reform in 1988, each Canadian taxpayer has between $1,600 and $1,800 more a year in his pocket. That too must be said! Because with the 1988 reform, taxes went down. Because with the reform in 1986 for the refundable federal sales tax credit, that tax, which as we know is not wonderful, is less regressive. With the GST, the credit will be raised and the tax will be even less regressive. The tax will penalize people on low or moderate incomes even less and it will

Government Orders
apply to those who can afford it. That is good, sound administration.
Look at the Leader of the Opposition. The Leader of the Opposition was asked if he was against the cuts to VTA Rail. Yes! Is he against free trade? Yes! Is he against the budget, all budgets? Is he against the GST? Yes! He is against all that. No problem! He is against it all. And I could go on. But we also say to him: Mr. Leader of the Opposition, if you are against it, fine! But what are your solutions?
He has none!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
"Well, no, I have no solutions, I am the opposition, I oppose. I have nothing to say, I am the opposition, I oppose." That is the policy of the Liberal Party: "to oppose!" Mr. Speaker, we do not create and continue to build a country with such a philosophy, "I oppose! I have nothing to say, I oppose!" That is the Opposition Leader's job. Since September 4, 1984, no Liberal or NDP Member has had the decency to come to this House and say, "I am against such and such a policy of the Conservative Government; here is what I propose. I am against a certain bill; I think it should be done this way." Not once has there been any suggestion on any subject. With such a style of opposition, we do not see how one of those two parties can govern this country the way it should be governed in the 1990s, as we approach the year 2000.
Because do not forget, Mr. Speaker, ten years from now we will be entering the year 2000, and to meet the expectations of Canadians for the year 2000 we need economic, cultural and social policies that are adequate.
Mr. Speaker, they suggest the Budget is no good. But like the four others that came before it, that Budget is Canada's economic policy. The Opposition never refers to the cost of the national debt for 1988-89-24.8 per cent of budget expenditures, nearly 25 per cent. This means that 25 per cent of all Canadian cheques issued by the Canadian Government are to pay the interests on the debts made by the previous Government opposite.
Mr. Speaker, to put that in terms of revenues, in other words if I take that 25 per cent and compare it against Canadian Government revenues for 1988-89, we come to 31.7 per cent!
That is 32 per cent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
-32 per cent, as stated by the Hon. Member for Abitibi (Mr. St-Julien). Indeed, 32 per cent of our fiscal revenues go to the payment, not of the principal, but the mere interests on our debts.
As we can easily understand, it is impossible to keep governing the country the way Opposition Parties would like to.
Mr. Speaker, last week I attended a yearly alumni meeting of Lafleche college, in Trois-Rivieres. It was the college's twentieth anniversary and I met a number of former students who are social workers, accountant or what have you, across Quebec. Do you know what those upwardly mobile young people said? They said: We believe in Canada, we believe that in order to have a strong country tomorrow, we need your economic policies now.
We believe that if VIA Rail cannot cover its costs, if it costs Canadians, if it costs us young people in this country $650 million a year, yes you must cut services!
Impossible!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, you must maintain it across the country, as you are now doing, but yes, you must cut services.
Unbelievable!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This, Mr. Speaker, is exactly what young Canadians are thinking!
Untrue!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The truth once more upsets people, Mr. Speaker, but we must live with it.
Mr. Speaker, they will have an opportunity after I conclude my speech to put questions if that is their wish. But if they will listen now, I will not be too long.
Mr. Speaker, last Saturday I attended a gathering of volunteers in Pointe-du-Lac, a yearly meeting of all those who give their time and energies to those activities. Those people receive no pay but they take their area, their community to heart. But what are these people
October 11, 1989

saying? They are saying the same thing: Indeed, the government in office has to administer and slash where it is needed, just so higher-income families will pay their fair share of taxes, much in the way lower-income families will also pay their fair share, but keeping in mind the fact that they do earn less.
Mr. Speaker, that is the rationale behind the GST. We know that the GST credit will be much higher than what it will be in 1990, but that year every adult will get $140 and every child $70, and the threshold will rise from $16,000 to $18,000 a year. That, Mr. Speaker, is sound administration.
I heard the NDP member refer to corporations and wealthy people who do not pay their share of taxes. As you would know, Mr. Speaker, since 1986 all Canadians pay at least a minimum tax, which means that there is no longer a single Canadian who does not pay his or her fair share of annual taxes.
You also know that as a result of the latest Budget the government will raise close to $1 billion more through the corporate surtax. Mr. Speaker, all corporations will pay their fair share of taxes. I would suggest this is sound management and, looking at it from an economic standpoint, that is what this country needs for the future.
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the former Minister of Finance refer to his performance. Here is his performance, Mr. Speaker: while he was Minister of Finance, average expenses increased by 20 per cent a year, the deficit went up, the net debt went up, everything went up when the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Timer) was Minister of Finance. This is the same man who today, as he has been doing over the past five years, is trying to teach ethics to this government which in four years did manage to reduce the annual deficit by $10 billion-a 25 per cent deficit reduction every year for four years. It stood at $39 billion when we took over, it is now down to $29 billion. Indeed, 39 minus 10 is 29, and 10 out of 39 works out to 25 per cent.
I see the opposition member smiling. The figures are there and, as my father would say, figures speak for themselves. Mr. Speaker, that is what the Budget is all about.
In 1991, again because we have to keep low income families in mind, as a result of the new federal sales tax
Government Orders
the annual refundable tax credit will amount to $275 per adult and $100 per child. Mr. Speaker, this tax will change absolutely nothing for families whose income is under $30,000. Nine million Canadians will receive a refundable tax credit. Nine million Canadians!
So when I see that the Opposition criticize a budget which shows economic leadership and is consistent with the efforts we have made over the past five years to reduce the deficit, to make sure that low income families are protected, to ensure that Canadian corporations can operate without tons of regulations and legislation as was the case under the previous government, to privatize Crown corporations which compete with private enterprise or which are not profit making concerns for the government- That is what we have done over the past four years and will continue to do, Mr. Speaker!
Bringing down the annual deficit is not wishful thinking but a necessity for this country. We just cannot imagine reaching Year 2000 with Canada being the country most in debt in the world. I think we must be realistic.
I want Members of the Opposition to start making serious proposals and stop arguing that they are against the budget, against the GST, against this or that. Members opposite are always behaving as though they were fighting for the survival of the country, involved in the very last struggle to help Canada make it-Mr. Speaker, we have been hearing the same tune for the past five years, and also for the past five years the Canadian economy has been doing fine, we have been creating jobs, the unemployment rate is down and Canadian men and women are living in a stable economic climate and enjoy pleasant federal-provincial relations. That is important too. Since 1984, major investments have been made throughout Canada, whether in the Atlantic provinces, Quebec, the prairies or British Columbia, and they have helped the economy. The unemployment rate will therefore go down. Mr. Speaker, these are realities.
In conclusion, I suggest that Bill C-28 must be adopted as soon as possible to be implemented and ensure that the economic well being which we have experienced since 1984 will continue.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for Abitibi on a question or comment.

Government Orders

A comment, Mr. Speaker. I am pleased to address the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres. You will recall that, in 1984, the Liberal Government then in power created a tax credit to promote research, thus causing the worst tax fraud in Canadian history, what could be called today the rip-off of the century. And today's Liberals, even the new ones, do not even remember it. They have not heard about it in their caucus. I would like to quote an article published in La Presse-

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Do you still have your Liberal party membership card?

That article dated September 30, 1987 reads as follows: "Taking into account the economic situation, the previous Liberal Government, for no valid reason, made taxpayers billions of dollars poorer." That was confirmed by Auditor General Dye. I want to get to Canada's current financial situation. In early 1984, Marc Lalonde the then Minister of Finance knew that the Scientific Research Tax Credit Program would cause problems. He was warned again a few months later but his Department did not do anything because the Government was about to go on the campaign trail.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell my hon. friend, the Member for Trois-Rivieres, that had the Liberal Government intervened right away in 1984, it could have saved a lot of money. And what did we do when we came into office? We cut those research tax credits. Finance Minister Marc Lalonde, who had predicted that the Program would cost $200 million, ended up with a $3.5 billion Program and a fraud of up to $1.9 billion. Nobody knows where that $1.9 billion went. My question for the Hon. Member for Trois-Rivieres is this: What could have been done in today's political context with $1.9 billion in his riding, in Abitibi, in Quebec and in Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to hear what I would call an astute question, and the hon. member for Abitibi.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if they want to ask questions, they're welcome to do so, but when I have the floor, I would like to be heard!
The hon. member for Abitibi is absolutely right. The former government implemented a program, and I have nothing against that except that it provides for tax credits, abatements, and so on. We know that when a back-door program, is established through the use of the
Income Tax Act instead of direct subsidies, it is impossible to predict its cost. They told us it would cost some $200 million, and that it would be promote scientific research, when in fact, Mr. Speaker, it did cost, as my colleague mentionned, almost $4 billion. But what's the problem, you ask. The then minister of Finance knew very well, right from the begining, that it would cost us plenty. But he stood behind his decision, and our country lost the opportunity to spend not millions, but billions of dollars, on social programs such as assistance programs for our handicapped or our ethnic groups, or on cultural and economic programs. Unfortunalety, that money has gone down the drain!

It goes to the heart of this country. It says a lot about what this country is. Is it a country of compassion? Is it a country that cares? Is it a country of citizens who feel that they are their brothers' keepers? Or is this a country where everyone is out for himself, where the rule of the jungle applies?
Those are the questions we have to ask ourselves. The answers are quite obvious. They are apparent from the presentations from the other side. We know where they stand. They want a society that can only be described as dog eat dog, everyone out for himself. That is what they want. That is why they are assaulting the seniors of this country. That is why they are going after the very men and women who built this country and who made this country what it is.
Just last week the chairman of the House of Commons finance committee managed, and it was quite a trick, to insult the entire population of western Canada. I think we got an apology from him. The Minister of State for Finance went one step further this afternoon. I am quite sure that he did not realize what he did nor did he intend to do it, but he managed to insult all senior citizens in this country. I will tell you how he did it. He did it by not

even mentioning the word "clawback". He did not even mention the subject. He did not allude to the issue.

Those people on the other side who form the government of the day know that the senior citizens in this country are angry. They are very, very upset. Leader of the Opposition this afternoon. They paid into a fund, and the government comes along and takes it. To add insult to injury, the Tories did not even ask, they did not even consult.
Was there a word about the clawback in the 1988 campaign? Not a whisper, not a boo, not a word. As soon as they got elected, what did they do? They put this infamous, perfidious, pernicious, ugly, nasty clawback into the budget, all in the name of deficit reduction. In fact, I got the feeling that the Conservatives have come to the conclusion that they can do anything, any damnable thing, any abominable thing, as long as it is in the name of deficit reduction. In fact, deficit reduction has been put up on a pedestal so high why, we might as well canonize it, make it a saint. Perhaps we should call it "Saint Deficit Reduction". Perhaps that is what the Tories want.
It is pretty shameful and they are not going to get away with it. They may use their majority, they may use their numbers, but they are going to pay for this because the seniors of this country are not going to forget. As far as I know, we still have a democracy in this country and as far as I know, we are going to have an election down the road. The senior citizens of this country are not going to forget.
Why does this government pick on seniors? Are they some kind of special group to be abused? They worked hard, put their money aside, they were expecting something and now this discrimination comes along, this discriminatory measure. If you reach a particular age, a particular plateau and if you have a particular level of income, they are going to hit you. I do not think that the government of the day is listening because there is unrest out there. We get telephone calls, we get letters, we get petitions. The people want to put a stop to this. There have been editorials written. I want to read into the record some remarks that were made in a publication entitled One Voice. It is the voice of senior citizens. There is an article in it called "Clawback Sparks National Outcry". I want to just pick out a few paragraphs because they put their argument against the clawback quite succinctly. I will not go into the preamble, but in the third paragraph, the article continues:
The same-or more-revenue could be generated by raising the rate at the top income tax bracket by only 1 percent, thereby taxing all high income earners.
In other words, if they think they need this money, they do not have to use a clawback. A mere 1 per cent on high income earners and they would get what they want.
The article continues:
Many view the mechanism as discriminatory, since it taxes pensioners and families at a higher rate than others earning the same income.
Of greater significance and concern is that over the years more and more pensioners and families will start repaying their benefits.
Partial indexation is responsible, the threshold is now $50,000, but by the year 2000 -
And that is only 11 years away.
-it will have fallen to the equivalent of $35,000 in today's dollars. By the time the Baby Boom generation enters retirement, most of them will have to repay their OAS benefits through the clawback.
That is what the seniors are saying. This is not the imagination of an opposition member. This does not come out of the blue. This is what the senior citizens of Canada are saying.
October 11, 1989

The article continues:
In the meantime, once we have accepted the principle of the clawback as part of our system, governments of the day are free to set the threshold as they wish -$30,000, $20,000, etc.

I want to repeat that because these are words of wisdom. I repeat:
History will remember the clawback as the end of universality, not for its drop in the deficit bucket.
Are government members listening? Are they paying any attention to what senior citizens are saying? Not a boo, not a word.
